questions.question: Which degree sequence is impossible for a simple graph because of the handshake lemma alone?
questions.explanation: 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 9 is odd, but the degrees must add up to 2|E|. The others have even sums and really exist: a triangle, two separate edges, and K4.

questions.question: A greedy coloring of a graph used 5 colors. Every vertex has degree at most 3. What happened?
options: This cannot happen: greedy always uses at most d + 1 = 4 colors here
The vertex order was unlucky, which is allowed
questions.explanation: Whatever the order, each vertex has at most 3 colored neighbors, so one of colors 1 to 4 is free. A bad order can waste colors, but it can never go beyond d + 1.

questions.question: In the inductive step of the d + 1 proof (induction on vertices), how should you begin?
options: Take an n-vertex graph and add a vertex to it
Take an arbitrary (n+1)-vertex graph with max degree at most d
Assume the claim for n + 1 and deduce it for n
questions.explanation: P(n+1) is a claim about ALL (n+1)-vertex graphs, so start from an arbitrary one. Building up from n vertices risks missing some graphs.

questions.question: A registrar wants the fewest exam slots for a big conflict graph. What is the realistic approach?
options: Run an efficient exact algorithm for the chromatic number
Use a heuristic like greedy coloring, since exact coloring is NP-complete
Use the four-color theorem to guarantee 4 slots
questions.explanation: Deciding whether even 3 colors suffice is NP-complete, so exact answers are out of reach for huge graphs. The four-color theorem only covers planar graphs, and conflict graphs usually aren't planar.
